opus-5.5.text:
Reward design has always been one of the dirtiest secrets in robotics and reinforcement learning. When people see a robot doing something impressive in simulation, they often don't see the weeks a PhD student spent hand-tuning a reward function: adding a term for this, penalizing that, adjusting a coefficient by 0.1, rerunning training overnight, and repeating. It's tedious, it requires a lot of domain expertise, and it doesn't scale. Every new task means starting that loop over again.

With Eureka we asked whether we could automate that loop with a large language model. The key insight is that reward functions are just code, and models like GPT-4 are very good at writing code. So we give the LLM the environment source code and a natural-language description of the task, and it writes candidate reward functions directly. Then we do something like evolutionary search. We sample a batch of reward functions, train policies with them in GPU-accelerated simulation, and feed the training statistics back to the LLM. We call this reward reflection. The model sees which reward components are actually being optimized and which aren't, and it revises the code. Over a few iterations it gets better and better.

What surprised us was that on most of the tasks we tried, Eureka's rewards matched or outperformed rewards written by human experts. And it unlocked things that were very hard to do by hand, like teaching a five-finger Shadow Hand to spin a pen the way people do at their desks. That's an extremely dexterous skill that would be very painful to reward-engineer manually.

Why do I think it's general-purpose? A few reasons.

First, it's task-agnostic. There's no robot-specific or task-specific template. You describe what you want in language, and the same pipeline works across very different robot bodies and skills.

Second, it's a nice division of labor between two kinds of intelligence. The LLM is great at high-level reasoning and semantics but terrible at fine-grained motor control. RL in simulation is the opposite. Eureka lets the LLM act as a teacher that writes the curriculum, and lets RL handle the low-level control. I think that pattern, a foundation model supervising a cheaper, faster learning process, will show up again and again.

Third, it scales with compute rather than human time. Simulation runs at thousands of times real time on GPUs, so you can explore far more reward candidates than any human could. And as the underlying language models improve, Eureka gets better for free, without us changing anything.

Finally, it keeps humans in the loop in the right way. You can give it feedback in plain language, like "the hand is moving too jerkily," and it will incorporate that into the next round. You move from writing reward code to just talking to the system about what you want.

So to me Eureka is a small, concrete example of a bigger idea: using foundation models to automate the parts of robot learning that used to need a human expert, so that we can eventually scale toward a general-purpose foundation agent.

r001.rationale: The response says Eureka automates the tedious, expertise-heavy process of hand-tuning reward functions by having an LLM write and revise them.

r002.rationale: The response describes generating reward functions for tasks provided in a natural-language description; it does not propose that Eureka generates new robot tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about Eureka is that it's really an example of a much bigger idea, which is: you can take an LLM and turn it into a kind of outer loop, a meta-optimizer, on top of a traditional optimization process.

Reward design in robotics has always been this weird, under-appreciated bottleneck. If you want a robot hand to spin a pen, you have to write a reward function, and that's actually a really hard problem. It's not just "did the pen rotate or not." You have to shape it. You have to decide how much to penalize the fingers for dropping the pen, how much to reward the angular velocity, how to balance all those terms. And historically that's been done by a grad student sitting there, tweaking coefficients, running the simulation overnight, looking at the result, and trying again. It's a very human-in-the-loop, very artisanal process.

What Eureka does is replace that human with GPT-4. We give the model the raw source code of the simulation environment, so it can actually see the state variables, the physics, what the robot can observe. And then we ask it to write the reward function as Python code. We don't do any task-specific prompting, we don't hand it templates. It just writes a bunch of candidate rewards, we train policies against all of them in parallel in Isaac Gym, and then we feed the training statistics back to the model, like "this term went up, this one plateaued, the success rate was this." And the model reflects on that and writes a better reward. And you just iterate.

The reason I think this is promising as a general technique, and not just a cute robotics trick, is a couple of things.

First, it works surprisingly well. On the tasks we tried, the rewards the LLM came up with were on average better than what human experts wrote, and on some tasks they were quite a bit better. And the pen-spinning result was the one that got people excited, because that's a task where nobody really had a good hand-designed reward before. It's the first time we saw a simulated five-finger hand do rapid pen spinning in a way that looks like what a human does.

Second, and this is the deeper point, the model is doing something that doesn't rely on it having a great world model of physics. It's doing it through trial and error with feedback from the actual training run. The LLM doesn't have to be right the first time. It just has to be a good hypothesis generator and a good critic of its own output when it sees the numbers. That's a very different use of an LLM than asking it to directly control a robot, where it would have to be correct at every step. Here it's operating at a much slower timescale, at the level of "how should we define what success means," and then gradient descent does the heavy lifting underneath.

And once you see it that way, you realize reward functions are just one instance. Anything where you have an inner optimization loop and an outer design loop that humans currently do by hand, you can try to put a language model in the outer loop. Curriculum design, environment design, choosing which skills to practice next, even hyperparameters. It's basically evolutionary search, but the mutation operator is a model that has read all of GitHub and can reason about why the last attempt didn't work. That's a much smarter mutation operator than random perturbation.

So that's why I'm excited about it. It's less about "LLM writes reward" and more about LLMs as a new kind of optimizer that can sit on top of all the other optimizers we already have.

r001.rationale: The response says reward design is a difficult, human-tweaked bottleneck and describes Eureka as replacing that human process with an LLM that writes and iterates on reward functions.

r002.rationale: The response mentions curriculum design and environment design as possible outer-loop applications, but does not clearly say Eureka could generate new robot tasks.

astra-6.text:
The key idea is that a reward function is a way of specifying what you want a robot to do. But writing a good one by hand is surprisingly difficult. You might want a robot hand to spin a pen, for example. How do you balance making progress, keeping a stable grip, and avoiding dropping it? Small choices in that reward can produce very different behaviors.

With Eureka, the language model writes the reward function as code. We then train the robot using reinforcement learning, evaluate what happens, and feed that feedback back to the language model so it can improve the reward. So the model proposes a solution, but simulation provides the test of whether it actually works.

What makes that general is that we’re not prescribing a separate reward-design procedure for every skill. The same loop can work across different robots and tasks. And you can incorporate human feedback in natural language—say, “That motion looks too jerky”—and have the model translate that into a change in the training objective.

I think that’s a powerful division of labor: the language model brings knowledge and the ability to write code, while reinforcement learning discovers the detailed motor behavior through experience.

r001.rationale: The response says the language model writes reward-function code and iteratively improves it from training feedback, framing this as avoiding a separate hand-designed procedure for each skill.

r002.rationale: It says the same reward-design loop can work across different robots and tasks, but does not say Eureka can generate new robot tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
The key idea is that a reward function is a way to communicate what we want a robot to do. But writing a good one by hand is surprisingly difficult. You might want a robot hand to spin a pen, but how do you translate that into a precise mathematical objective without accidentally rewarding some strange shortcut?

With Eureka, the language model writes that reward function as code. We train the robot using it, give the model feedback about what worked and what failed, and let it revise the code. So you have this iterative loop where the LLM proposes an objective and reinforcement learning tests it through interaction with the environment.

What makes that promising as a general technique is that the model doesn’t need to produce every motor command. It operates at the level of specifying what success looks like, while reinforcement learning figures out how to achieve it. That gives us a way to connect high-level knowledge in language models with low-level skills learned through experience. And because the interface is code, we can apply that same basic loop across many different tasks.

r001.rationale: It says a language model writes and revises reward-function code, but does not state that this automates engineering that otherwise requires human robotics expertise.

r002.rationale: It says the approach can apply across many different tasks, but does not propose generating new robot tasks.
